hints: Think about what happens to the very ends of a linear chromosome each time DNA is copied - can the copying machinery reach right to the tip?
If a little bit of DNA is lost from the tip each cycle, what would be the danger if that tip contained important genes?
Apart from losing information, how might a bare chromosome end be mistaken by the cell for something dangerous like a broken chromosome?
walkthrough:
Why chromosome ends are a problem**
Linear eukaryotic chromosomes cannot be fully replicated right to the end, so a short piece of DNA is lost from the tip at each round of DNA replication. Without a buffer this would soon eat into useful DNA.

Telomeres as disposable buffers**
Telomeres are repetitive, non-coding sequences at both ends. They do not code for proteins, so losing part of a telomere does no harm. This allows cells to carry out many continuous mitoses and cell cycles before essential genes are threatened.

Protecting stability**
By capping the ends, telomeres prevent loss of genes / genetic information and stop the sticky ends fusing together or being recognised by repair enzymes as damaged, broken DNA.

Final answer: Allow many rounds of DNA replication / mitosis; telomeres are lost instead of genes / coding sequences, preventing loss of genetic information; prevent chromosome ends fusing or being recognised as damaged DNA.

hints: Remember the pairing rules used when mRNA is made on a DNA template: A pairs with U, T pairs with A, C pairs with G.
walkthrough:
Pair each DNA base with its RNA partner**
Use the template A A T C C C. A pairs with U, T pairs with A, C pairs with G in RNA. So A-A-T-C-C-C becomes U-U-A-G-G-G.
Final answer: U U A G G G

hints: Fig. 5.3 uses triplets on the non-transcribed (coding) strand, which match the mRNA sequence except T is used instead of U - so first convert your RNA back to that DNA form.
Split the six-base sequence into two triplets from the start, then read the wheel from the centre outwards with first base in the centre.
walkthrough:
Get the coding-strand triplets**
Your TERRA RNA is $UUA-GGG$. The non-transcribed coding strand has the same sequence but with T in place of U, so $TTA-GGG$. The transcribed strand shown in Fig. 5.1 is the complement $AAT-CCC$.

Read the wheel for each triplet**
Start at the centre with the first base, move to the middle ring for the second base, then the outer ring for the third base. $TTA$: first T, second T, third A gives leucine. $GGG$: first G, second G, third G gives glycine.

hints: Link more transcription to what happens next in gene expression - what new molecules and then what new functional molecules will the cell be able to make?
walkthrough:
From more transcripts to more functions**
If many more genes are transcribed, many more different mRNA molecules are made and then translated into many more different proteins and enzymes. In a stem cell this extra range of proteins allows the cell to become differentiated / specialised to take on a particular function, and to grow and make new organelles before dividing.

Final answer: Increase in number of different proteins / enzymes / mRNA molecules produced, allowing cell to differentiate / specialise; or increased growth / organelle production in preparation for mitosis.
